item.title: Xi says China ready to work with Kyrgyzstan to enhance alignment of development strategies
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-31
Xi says China ready to work with Kyrgyzstan to enhance alignment of development strategies BISHKEK -- President Xi Jinping said Monday that China stands ready to work with Kyrgyzstan to better align development strategies, deepen exchanges of experience in governance, deliver more tangible and accessible outcomes of practical cooperation, and make substantive progress in building a China-Kyrgyzstan community with a shared future. Xi said in his opening remarks when meeting with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov that under their guidance, bilateral relations have made a leap forward, with cooperation flourishing across all areas in recent years. Major cooperation projects with Kyrgyzstan, including the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, have progressed steadily in recent years, providing effective support for the development of both countries, benefiting their people and promoting peace, stability and prosperity in the region, Xi said.

item.title: More Kyrgyz youths opt for Mandarin tests
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-31
More Kyrgyz youths opt for Mandarin tests Candidates rush to embrace broader opportunities as bilateral ties flourish The number of people appearing for Mandarin proficiency tests in Kyrgyzstan has surged more than threefold over the past five years, reflecting a growing interest in the Chinese language amid deepening economic ties and educational cooperation between the two countries, the administrator of the HSK examination said. Li Peize, general manager of Chinese Testing International Co, which administers the exam, said the total number of HSK candidates across all levels grew from 3,139 in 2021 to 12,611 in 2025 in Kyrgyzstan. According to Li, in the first half of the year, more than 7,600 candidates took the test, with the annual total expected to exceed 15,000. The number is projected to surpass 20,000 by 2028, making Kyrgyzstan the first Central Asian country to reach that milestone, he said. He said that Kyrgyzstan's interest in China shows that the bilateral relationship has entered a golden era. "Economic and trade needs have created a broad market, policy support has built a solid bridge, and the desire to study in China and cultural identification have injected endless vitality," he added. China has become a major source of investment in Kyrgyzstan. Major projects — from hydropower stations and ski resorts to financial investment zones — have created abundant local job opportunities, Li said. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan Railway and cross-border e-commerce have further fueled demand for professionals with both Chinese-language skills and technical expertise, he added. The Chinese Embassy in Kyrgyzstan has for years run a scholarship program that requires applicants for full scholarships to have completed at least HSK Level 3. Four Confucius Institutes and more than 20 Confucius classrooms have been established in the Central Asian nation, along with a Luban Workshop and a Silk Road School for cross-border e-commerce — initiatives that link language learning with vocational training and employment, he said. Li noted that a growing number of young Kyrgyz people also consider Chinese as a gateway to better opportunities. China's world-class educational resources, increasingly convenient visa policies and transportation links have made studying in China more attractive than ever. The profile of Chinese learners in Kyrgyzstan has also diversified. Test-takers now include university students, civil servants, translators, business professionals and skilled workers — evidence that Chinese is shifting from a cultural interest to a practical tool for career advancement, he added. For many Kyrgyz students, learning Chinese has opened doors to new experiences and opportunities in China. Ayana Bazarkulova, 20, a student at Beijing Foreign Studies University, said that she has been interested in Chinese culture since childhood. After two years in China, she described the country as "highly developed and modern, especially in terms of technology". "Almost everything can be done online — shopping, ordering food and paying bills, by using digital payment systems. It makes daily life very convenient and efficient," she said. Bazarkulova added that Chinese people are "friendly, kind and welcoming" toward international students. Having studied Chinese for nearly three years, she finds the language fascinating. "The Chinese characters are very interesting, each with its own meaning and history. I also like the tones because they make the language different from many others," she said. Erkemai Zarylbekova, 19, a student at Beijing International Studies University, said that her older sister inspired her to learn Chinese. After two years of study, she said China is a modern, safe and convenient country to be in with its excellent public transportation and advanced technology. "Chinese people have always been friendly and helpful to me. Even when my Chinese was not very good, many people were patient and encouraged me," she said. Nuraiym Aibekova, 27, a second-year PhD student at the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing, first came to China in 2018. She returned to campus in 2023 and said China has become "like a second home". She praised the country's safety, cleanliness and convenience — from online shopping to efficient public transportation. She passed HSK Level 4 after only four months of intensive study and later obtained levels 5 and 6. "At first, I learned Chinese because it was necessary for my studies and daily life," she said. "However, as my language skills improved, I realized that Chinese opened many new opportunities for me." zoushuo@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Social media fuels Chinese yoga wear boom
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-31
Amid the global yoga culture boom, Chinese yoga wear brands have expanded overseas and found favor with international consumers. On TikTok, a young girl from the United States shared her thoughts on her recently discovered favorite brand CRZ YOGA — a sportswear brand from Guangzhou, Guangdong province. In front of the camera, she tried on four sets of yoga wear. "The quality is good. The material is super light. I like the texture of the clothes. The color is what I look for. I wear CRZ YOGA to the gym every day," she said. The video received thousands of likes and comments, and many other users also praised the Chinese brand. Ashton and Ryan, a couple from the US, tried on yoga wear together on a video posted on TikTok. "I already went to the gym today, but I feel like going to the gym again," Ashton said. They also favor yoga wear from Halara — another Chinese brand. Relying on a mature flexible supply chain in China, domestic yoga clothing brands have established a high cost-effectiveness advantage. With platforms such as TikTok and Instagram, they are gaining popularity among overseas consumers. On US online shopping giant Amazon, CRZ YOGA performs well, often occupying nearly half of the top 10 spots on the women's yoga pants bestseller list, and often taking the top spot on the women's sports short skirt list. Among its products, the high-waisted nude yoga leggings priced at $26 are the best-selling product under the brand, with over 26,000 user reviews on Amazon alone. Additionally, CRZ YOGA has also expanded its men's clothing line. To enhance visibility and trust, CRZ YOGA has established a matrix of Instagram, TikTok and YouTube accounts in social media marketing, producing content based on the characteristics of different platforms. On TikTok, it collaborates with small — and medium-sized influencers to shoot "one outfit, multiple wear" lifestyle videos, and showcase the versatility of products and achieving significant results. According to data from market researcher Jungle Scout, one of the brand's $32 yoga pants sold more than 80,000 units on TikTok in a month, with a monthly revenue of $2.84 million. Halara, a sportswear company based in Beijing, entered the US market in 2023. It opened several official TikTok accounts, including a main account with 700,000 followers, with content focused on dressing up and interacting with cute pets. Its popular topics have drawn more than 1 billion views. Data from cross-border information platform Crosspie revealed that Halara ranked second in sales in the US sportswear category on TikTok in March 2025 and topped the charts in April. The total sales of its four small stores in the US exceeded $63 million, and its flagship store Halara US has been ranked first in TikTok's sports and outdoor categories for four consecutive months. Influencers account for 58.23 percent of total sales. The independent website has received more than 13 million visits in the past three months, with 84.46 percent of the traffic coming from the US. Gabby Hirata, president of Halara, said that going forward, the company will adjust the marketing style and content on social media, while increasing a new round of brand building. "Our website will be optimized and adjusted based on the brand's tone and user habits. "Also, we will continue to diversify our content creator team and continue to release some guidelines to encourage users to share what they want completely freely," she said. Lin Xianping, executive deputy secretary-general of China Urban Expert Think Tank Committee, and associate professor at Hangzhou City University, said: "The reason behind domestic yoga clothing brands quickly opening up overseas markets is the flexible supply chain in China. Also, scenario-based product positioning meets the real consumption needs overseas, with high cost-effectiveness forming a strong market penetration, and short-video social media model reconstructing the overseas marketing path." According to data from China Sporting Goods Federation, China's export value of sports equipment reached $28.39 billion in 2024, a year-on-year increase of 6.77 percent.

item.title: The SCO at 25: Dialogue over division
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-31
The SCO at 25: Dialogue over division Share - WeChat
Leaders of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization are gathering in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. When the SCO was founded in 2001, its primary mission was addressing regional security challenges. Yet over the past two and a half decades, its agenda spans far beyond security, encompassing economic integration, digital infrastructure, connectivity, and people-to-people exchanges. The SCO's greatest achievement over the past 25 years is not simply its expanding membership. It is the powerful precedent it sets: proving that dialogue and cooperation can prevail over division. In a world increasingly fragmented by geopolitical tensions, the SCO offers a practical model for peaceful coexistence and mutual development.

Chinese consumption moves from 'buying' to 'experiencing' Share - WeChat
The consumption trend among Chinese consumers has shifted from "buying" to "experiencing" this summer — with soccer chants and desert stargazing emerging as the new spending currency in 2026. From 450-million-yuan ($60.93 million) targeted vouchers to visa-free entry and instant departure tax refunds, a converging policy toolkit is injecting sustained momentum into the experience economy.

item.title: Global Civilization Initiative boosts cross-cultural exchanges
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-31
Former Egyptian PM: Global Civilization Initiative boosts cross-cultural exchanges This year marks the 70th anniversary of China-Egypt diplomatic ties. In a recent interview with China Daily, former Egyptian prime minister Essam Sharaf described the Global Civilization Initiative as a cornerstone for building trust through dialogue and exchanges. "These two civilizations, Chinese and Egyptian, form a good part of the human history," Sharaf said. As the founder of the Sharaf Foundation for Sustainable Development and the winner of the inaugural Orchid Award, Sharaf believes people-to-people connectivity lies at the heart of civilizational exchange. Looking ahead, he hopes to build a cultural hub for the Arab world, so China and Egypt may shine as beacons of global civilization. "I feel like the two countries deserve to be enlightening points in the world," he said. Watch the video!

item.title: Live: Rescue teams intensify searches in Gyirong
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-31
President Xi Jinping urges all-out rescue, relief efforts after mudslide hits border port in Xizang Level-II emergency response activated after mudslide hits border port in Xizang BEIJING -- As of Aug 30, all Chinese nationals who had been contacted in the disaster-stricken areas of Nepal after a devastating mudslide have been properly transferred and resettled, and they were safe, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said Monday. Spokesperson Guo Jiakun told a daily media briefing that currently, China is making every effort to search for and rescue the missing at home and abroad, and is in close contact with foreign embassies in China to jointly conduct screening and aftermath handling for missing foreign nationals. The disaster, triggered by a sudden glacier collapse in Nepal's border area, has caused significant casualties and left people missing on both Chinese and Nepali sides. It has been the most serious cross-border disaster between the two countries in recent years, and the relief efforts are unprecedentedly complex and arduous. Three Wing Loong drones have provided more than 3,900 emergency calls in the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port area in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, as rescue teams work to restore communications and assess disaster conditions, according to the Ministry of Emergency Management. The mudslide struck Gyirong Port in Gyirong county on Aug 26 after originating on the Nepalese side of the China-Nepal border. It severely damaged roads leading to the port and disrupted electricity and telecommunications, complicating rescue operations. Following the disaster, the Ministry of Emergency Management and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology immediately deployed the drones to support emergency command communications and disaster reconnaissance. As of noon on Monday, the drones had logged more than 130 flight hours and supported more than 3,900 calls, the Ministry of Emergency Management said. The drones established emergency communications coverage over the disaster zone, providing a vital link for rescue teams operating in areas where ground-based communications infrastructure had been damaged. Operations have been complicated by the area's high altitude, low temperatures, turbulent air currents in mountain valleys and rapidly changing weather conditions. To maintain continuous coverage, flight crews adopted a range of operating methods, including remote takeoffs and landings from different locations, long-distance repositioning and simultaneous operations by two aircraft over the same area. These measures enabled the drones to reach designated areas quickly and work together to maintain emergency communications support, according to the ministries. In addition to providing communications services, the drones have continued to conduct aerial reconnaissance over the affected area, supplying information to support risk assessments and emergency command decisions. Doctors providing psychological support and traditional Tibetan therapies at a temporary shelter in Gyirong town are helping evacuees cope with fear and sleep problems following the severe mudslide that hit Gyirong Port on Wednesday. They are also continuing health screenings for elderly people and children. The massive mudslide, originating on the Nepali side of the border, struck the Gyirong Port area in Gyirong county, Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, at around 10:30 am on Wednesday. As of 6 pm on Saturday, the disaster had left 16 people dead and 546 others missing, according to regional authorities. A total of 499 residents from five at-risk villages have been relocated to temporary shelters converted from hotels and guesthouses. Lhawang Tsering, a doctor from the Shigatse Tibetan Medicine Hospital, was dispatched to Gyirong to provide psychological support and Tibetan medical care. The four-member medical team left Shigatse on Wednesday, arrived in Gyirong at around 11 pm, and began working at the shelter the following morning. The shelter mainly accommodates residents evacuated from Trungsi village in Gyirong town and Kopa village in Salhe township. "Some elderly residents witnessed the disaster and were deeply frightened," Lhawang Tsering said. "They were constantly worried that another disaster might occur." Some evacuees had difficulty sleeping or became irritable, while a small number experienced episodes of crying or fainting, Lhawang Tsering said. Some elderly residents also have underlying conditions such as high blood pressure. The medical team has prioritized screenings for vulnerable residents, particularly elderly people and those whose relatives were affected by or remain missing after the disaster. Two local doctors on the team provide general medical diagnosis and treatment, while the other two members focus on psychological support and traditional Tibetan therapies. In addition to counseling, doctors have used Horme therapy — a traditional Tibetan treatment similar to moxibustion — and Tibetan medicinal incense to help residents relax and ease emotional distress. Lhawang Tsering said the overall emotional state of evacuees had stabilized following the interventions, and no further episodes of crying or fainting had been reported. The team is continuing to screen residents for common illnesses such as colds and diarrhea and to identify anyone who may need to be transferred to a higher-level hospital. None of the evacuated residents at the shelter was physically injured in the disaster, Lhawang Tsering said. However, the large number of elderly people and children means that regular health monitoring and targeted care remain necessary. Rescuers had reopened the main access route to within 1.2 kilometers of the border gate at Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, by early Monday, as authorities prepared to intensify a new round of searches in the core disaster area, according to the frontline rescue headquarters. A massive mudslide originating on the Nepalese side of the China-Nepal border struck Gyirong Port on Wednesday morning, causing major casualties and leaving people missing. The disaster severely damaged National Highway G216, the main road leading to the port, and cut electricity and communications. The rescue headquarters said at a news conference on Sunday that rescuers were pushing southward along G216 from the northern side of Gyirong Port to reopen the route while searching for survivors and missing people along the route. On Monday, China Anneng Group deployed 150 emergency rescue personnel and 29 sets of various mechanical equipment to the operation. As of 8 am Monday, crews had advanced another 508 meters. The road remains a key access point for rescuers attempting to reach the hardest-hit area of Gyirong Port. Progress has also been made in restoring communications. The first emergency base station close to the border gate at Gyirong Port began operating at 1:30 pm Sunday, extending communication coverage toward the core rescue area. From the catastrophic collapse of a glacier at 5,200 meters in Nepal to the debris flow crashing into the valley at Gyirong Port, roughly 1,800 meters above sea level, it took just seven minutes to cover 22 kilometers at an average speed of 50 meters per second. This mudslide was larger, faster, and more powerful, leaving downstream communities with an extremely narrow window to evacuate and causing even more devastating destruction and casualties. The first thing that struck Li Jinchong, a heavy machinery operator from the Chinese military, when arriving near the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in the Xizang autonomous region was the scale of the disaster. "The roads were damaged and the mountain slopes bore scars of torrents of mud and ice sweeping through," he said. "It was different from seeing the catastrophe on the news. I felt shock and pain." This is Li's first deployment to a natural disaster of this scale. The 32-year-old soldier from the second mobile corps of the People's Armed Police Force has had seven years of experience operating excavators, wheel loaders and other heavy machines, though mostly for clearing ice and snow blocking transportation during freezing winters. "I am used to the barren high plateaus, with gentle rolling mountains that stretch out," he said. "Here, it's different. The mountains are forested, steep and more imposing. Stepping in here, I can feel the tightness of the slopes as if they are closing in on us." This is the narrow, treacherous space where Li and his fellow soldiers now operate. Sent to assist rescue operations for hundreds of people missing after the mudslide that hit Gyirong Port in Shigatse city's Gyirong county on Wednesday morning, their key mission is clearing debris and restoring transport on a stretch of highway leading to the hard-hit border crossing. Despite the unfamiliar terrain, Li said he is confident operating the machine safely and efficiently, drawing on his rich experience with excavation and a determination to get the job done in harsh conditions. Li was an undergraduate student in visual communication design from Yunnan province in Southwest China before joining the armed forces in 2018. He said before moving from drawing to operating heavy machinery, he had resolved to excel in the discipline, spending day and night learning the intricacies of every machine he touched and honing his skills in complicated conditions, often marked by gusting winds and bone-chilling snow. Now, that hard-won knowledge is being put to use again. At the site near Gyirong Port, he works by shaving tall piles of debris from the top down in layers, lowering the height gradually. "The soil is loose here, so it is important to maintain a safe distance from the edge at all times to prevent tipping the machine or triggering a collapse," he said. A key facet of becoming a proficient machine operator is guaranteeing safety. Operating an excavator carries many risks. For instance, accidentally striking the excavator bucket on steel or hard rock buried in the mud could cause fragments to bounce as high as three meters, shattering the operator's windshield and endangering people nearby. When operating wheel loaders, hitting pieces of rebar or fencing underneath can puncture tires. Blind spots around such large machines are also a constant concern. Years of hands-on practice have enabled Li to internalize safety protocols. "It is like we have developed muscle memory and are wired to stay on high alert when working to ensure absolute safety," he added. Ensuring safety is also part of the motto that guides the work of Zhang Qiang, a 38-year-old armed forces soldier who has also joined the mission in Gyirong county. "Carefully selecting the machine's operating position and constantly making adjustments to prevent mud churning, and being aware of the risk of falling rocks from prolonged rainfall are among the hazards we should watch out for here," he said. Zhang participated in rescue operations after the 8.1-magnitude earthquake in Nepal in 2015, as well as a number of domestic emergency road repair missions. Compared to his level of expertise more than a decade ago, Zhang said he has found himself to have become more mature and patient, especially in acute circumstances. "This is also a team effort. With everyone pulling together and cooperation between units getting smoother, we are making progress day by day," he said. Thousands of netizens have left messages of support on the social media account of the local border inspection station in the Xizang autonomous region, after a mudslide originating in Nepal hit Gyirong Port in Shigatse on Wednesday, leaving personnel out of contact. The official WeChat account of the Xizang general station of entry and exit border inspection, which oversees Gyirong Port, said on Saturday that it had been inundated with messages, prayers and good wishes from netizens across the country since Wednesday. The post also featured a short video of officers at Gyirong Port. As of Sunday afternoon, the video had received about 130,000 likes, been forwarded over 11,200 times and had about 12,000 comments. One netizen, with the username "Nanshanxianke", commented on the video: "They (the station officers) guard the nation's gateway with their lives." Others responded with prayers, saying, "May a miracle be with them, and may they all return safely." "They are the pillars of their families. This is a tragedy for so many households," wrote a netizen named "Hezhouhuaer". Another user, "Wuxibancaijiejie", posted a photo of a young woman in uniform sitting on a sofa, with a caption that read: "We are all waiting for you to come back. You have never made us worry during your more than a decade of service at the border. We believe you will return safely this time too. Your 1-year-old son calls out 'mom' every day." Netizen "Yanjun" wrote: "Tears welled up in my eyes. Though we are strangers to one another, our hearts are connected. You are the people I respect the most." The station concluded the post with an appeal for hope: "We seek no grand ode to heroism — only a miracle that endures. May it come, and may our fellow officers return safely." caoyin@chinadaily.com.cn A total of 261 foreign nationals remained unaccounted for after a massive mudslide hit a border port in Gyirong county, Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, local authorities said on Sunday. The foreigners, from 23 countries, include 104 from Nepal, 49 from India, 18 from the United States, 15 from the United Kingdom, six from Canada, six from Australia, four from South Africa and three from Russia. The figures were announced at a news conference held by the regional government's information office, following joint searches and the cross-checking of information by authorities responsible for foreign affairs, public security, culture and tourism and emergency management. After multiple rounds of inspections and population verification at the border port, no foreign tourists remained in Gyirong county, said Zhao Peng, vice-chairman of the regional government. According to Zhao, who also serves as the deputy head of the disaster emergency and rescue command headquarters, the sudden and severe mudslide caused extensive damage to infrastructure and personnel records in the affected area, significantly hampering efforts to trace and verify information about those who are unaccounted for. He said information on the unaccounted-for foreign nationals had been reported to their respective embassies. Two 24-hour English-language hotlines — 0086-891-6817165 and 0086-183-08026705 — have also been established for the families of the missing foreign nationals. Foreign nationals currently registered in the county are primarily Nepali border residents, cross-border vehicle crews and Nepali individuals involved in international marriages, all of whom are safe, Zhao added. "For Nepali border residents wishing to return to their home country, we will carry out transfer, transportation and customs clearance processes in a careful and orderly manner," he said. "For those who voluntarily choose to stay in Xizang, we will provide security and living support." He emphasized that staff members will consistently respect the wishes and reasonable demands of the Nepali side, adhering to the principles of friendly consultation and prioritizing humanitarian needs. A thorough evaluation will also be conducted to assess the departure needs of foreign tourists in Xizang, Zhao said, adding that authorities will facilitate their exit through ports in Lhasa, Burang and Zhangmu while ensuring their safe and smooth departure. Additionally, communication with embassies in China will be maintained and strengthened to report work progress in a timely manner, he added. Contact the writers at caoyin@chinadaily.com.cn China delivered 50 metric tons of emergency relief supplies to Nepal on Sunday and dispatched nine tunnel rescue experts to assist with rescue operations following a deadly mudslide on Wednesday. According to the Chinese embassy in Nepal, two Y-20 transport aircraft operated by the People's Liberation Army Air Force carrying 13,200 relief supplies arrived at Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu on Sunday morning. The supplies included tents, blankets, sleeping bags, compressed food items and first-aid kits. They will be distributed in disaster-hit areas to help meet the basic living and emergency medical needs of those affected. Four Chinese tunnel rescue experts and their equipment arrived in Kathmandu with the supplies, while five others had already reached the disaster area by helicopter from Gyirong county in China's Xizang autonomous region on Saturday and begun working at a hydropower station. The delivery of relief supplies and the expert missions marked the latest progress in implementing China's assistance package for Nepal, which Foreign Minister Wang Yi said during a phone call with his Nepali counterpart Shisir Khanal on Saturday included emergency cash assistance and humanitarian aid. Wang said a sudden glacier collapse in the China-Nepal border area had triggered severe mudslides, causing significant casualties and leaving people missing on both sides. He described it as the most serious cross-border disaster between the two countries in recent years, adding that the complexity and difficulty of the rescue and relief operations were unprecedented. Wang said a meeting of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee had called for emergency aid to Nepal's disaster-hit areas and international rescue cooperation, noting that it was an important political decision reflecting China's friendship with Nepal. China has also shared important information with Nepal, including imagery, satellite and hydrological data from the disaster-hit area, as well as early-warning information on upstream barrier lakes, Wang said. Regarding Nepali citizens stranded on the Chinese side, Wang said China had made proper arrangements for them and would help them return to Nepal as soon as possible. He thanked Nepal for its efforts to rescue and evacuate Chinese citizens in need, expressing hope that the Nepali side would continue such efforts. In the face of the disaster, Wang called on China and Nepal to stand firmly together, work together to overcome the difficulties and demonstrate their traditional friendship across the Himalayas through concrete actions. Khanal expressed sincere gratitude for China's emergency humanitarian assistance. He said that although both Nepal and China had been affected by the disaster, China had overcome its own difficulties to convey sympathy and provide assistance to Nepal at the earliest opportunity, fully demonstrating the high level of Nepal-China relations. Nepal will continue to work closely with China and make every effort to rescue Chinese nationals who remain trapped or missing, while working together to locate and rescue all missing foreign nationals, Khanal said. He added that Nepal is ready to strengthen cooperation with China and further advance the strategic partnership between the two countries through post-disaster reconstruction and efforts to prevent and mitigate disasters, including responses to climate change. Figures released by Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority showed that workers had recovered 734 human remains from mudslide-hit areas as of 9 am local time on Sunday, with 2,498 people still missing. zhaojia@chinadaily.com.cn BEIJING -- Gyirong county in Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region is expected to see more rainfall in the coming days, with significant nighttime precipitation, the National Meteorological Center said on Sunday. From Sunday to Monday, Gyirong will experience light to moderate rain, and on Tuesday, it will see moderate to heavy rain at night, according to the forecast. The rain comes as rescue and relief efforts are accelerating after a mudslide struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border on Aug 26. A yellow alert for geological disaster risks, the third tier in China's four-level warning system, was jointly issued at 6 pm by the Ministry of Natural Resources and the China Meteorological Administration. It warned of relatively high risks in parts of southern Xizang, including the Gyirong area, from 8 pm Sunday to 8 pm Monday. Meteorological authorities advised caution over the next few days in the Gyirong Port area due to rainfall and elevated geological disaster risks. Drivers of rescue vehicles are urged to watch for slippery roads on routes from Xigaze to Gyirong and from Gyirong to Gyirong Port. The collapse of a high-altitude glacier in Nepal triggered a deadly mudslide at a major China-Nepal border crossing. Experts said the underlying instability may be linked to a warming climate that is rapidly altering glaciers, permafrost and mountain slopes across the Himalayas. The disaster occurred on Wednesday morning on the Nepal side of the border, sending a torrent of ice, rocks and debris toward Gyirong Port in Gyirong county, a major land crossing linking China and Nepal in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region. The mudslide caused heavy casualties and left hundreds missing in China. It was triggered by the collapse of a glacier at an elevation of about 5,200 meters on the southern slope of Langtang Lirung in Nepal. The glacier broke apart at about 10:52 am on Wednesday, triggering an icerock avalanche, the Xizang regional government said on Sunday. The avalanche rapidly descended to an elevation of about 4,000 meters, scouring the mountain slope and generating a massive debris flow. It traveled 22 kilometers in seven minutes before reaching Gyirong Port, at an elevation of about 1,800 meters. The disaster flattened about 0.7 square kilometers of the area and destroyed 27 buildings and associated facilities, authorities said. The findings were based on an analysis of remote-sensing data and information transmitted from the disaster site, combined with field inspections and interviews conducted by a cryosphere emergency disaster mitigation team from the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment in Chengdu, Sichuan province. Xu Qiang, president of Chengdu University of Technology, said the disaster's extreme destructive power was driven by geological factors, including the huge elevation drop of more than 3,000 meters. The massive volume of debris and the sudden onset of the collapse also left little time for warning or response, Xu said. The US Geological Survey similarly found that the disaster was likely triggered by a rapid slope failure involving a glacier in the Langtang National Park in Nepal. Ben Mirus, a research geologist with the USGS, said glacier collapses combined with debris avalanches are relatively uncommon, but large landslides and rockfalls can cause devastating damage. However, while scientists have identified the immediate mechanism, they have yet to determine why the glacier and surrounding rock became unstable and collapsed at that particular moment. "It's really hard to attribute the exact trigger for this particular glacial collapse," Mirus said. According to local meteorological data, there was no heavy rainfall near the outlet of the debris flow at the time of the disaster, making it unlikely that intense rainfall alone could explain the event. Fan Xuanmei, director of the State Key Laboratory of Geohazard Prevention and Geoenvironment Protection at Chengdu University of Technology, said that, based on current evidence, the collapse was likely the result of a combination of the region's geological setting and a warming climate. The Himalayas are located along the collision boundary between the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates. Continued tectonic activity has fractured mountain rock and contributed to frequent earthquakes, leaving slopes vulnerable to failure. "Against this long-term tectonic backdrop, climate warming is acting as an important 'amplifier'," Fan said. She added that rising temperatures are accelerating the melting of snow and ice, intensifying freeze-thaw weathering of rock and reducing the stability of snow cover and glaciers, "thereby increasing the likelihood of large-scale avalanches, glacier collapse and rockfalls". As glaciers retreat, they can also expose and leave behind large quantities of loose rock and sediment that can later be mobilized by a collapse, she said. Since the Industrial Revolution, the world has warmed by about 1.4 C, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service. China Meteorological Administration data shows that the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau's average temperature increased by 0.37 C per decade between 1961 and 2022, faster than global and national averages. The changing climate is also affecting the region's water systems. The area of lakes in 12 major river basins on the plateau increased 36.7 percent from 1990 to 2020, according to the administration. Experts warn that these changes can create interconnected hazards rather than isolated disasters. "Detecting such failures before they occur is extremely difficult," Fan said. Potential source areas are often above 5,000 meters, where conventional field monitoring is difficult. Satellite observations can be limited by snow and ice cover and steep terrain, while monitoring equipment has to operate in extreme cold and high-altitude conditions. "We also lack mature models capable of reliably predicting the complete chain from glacier or rock collapse to debris flow, mudslide and downstream flooding," she said. The disaster also revealed gaps in cross-border monitoring. The debris flow reached China from the apparent source in Nepal within minutes, leaving little time for information to be transmitted to communities downstream. "After the disaster, we immediately contacted experts in Nepal, but they also lacked data from relevant weather stations to confirm the conditions at the site," Fan said. The changing Himalayan environment has made cooperation increasingly important, experts said. China and Nepal could jointly build high-altitude meteorological and hydrological monitoring stations, share satellite remote-sensing and seismic data and establish rapid cross-border disaster notification mechanisms, Fan said. Such efforts could also expand across the Himalayas, bringing together China, Nepal, India, Pakistan and international research institutions to develop shared monitoring networks and early-warning technologies, she added. Contact the writers at zhaoyimeng@chinadaily.com.cn Rescue teams are advancing by air, land and water routes into the hardest-hit area of the Gyirong border port in Gyirong county, Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, as search operations for hundreds of people missing after Wednesday's devastating mudslide were stepped up. The disaster has so far left 16 people dead and 546, including 261 foreigners, missing. In a major development, the first emergency communication base station at the Gyirong port was put into operation on Sunday afternoon. Located 1.2 kilometers from the border gate, the base station fills a communication coverage gap, providing stable and reliable support for rescue operations, road clearance, material transportation and front-line workers, Xinhua reported. Communication signals have reached the core rescue site, Nyima Dorje, head of the region's communications administration, said on Sunday. According to regional authorities, 499 residents from five at-risk villages had been evacuated to hotels and guesthouses. Gama Cedain, chairman of the Xizang regional government and head of the emergency rescue headquarters, said the region activated its highest-level emergency responses shortly after the mudslide struck on Wednesday. So far, 2,141 personnel from the People's Liberation Army, armed police, fire and rescue services, border defense and public security authorities, as well as from China Anneng Group, have been mobilized, along with 269 rescue vehicles and 3,922 sets of equipment, Gama Cedain said. Ren Wei, executive vice-chairman of the regional government, said the rescue operations have been complicated by unstable geological conditions. The disaster severely damaged National Highway G216, the main route to the Gyirong port. "The overall difficulty level of the rescue operation is far more than in a conventional geological disaster," Ren said. Rescue teams opened a mountain route and used ropes to lower firefighters into the core area. Engineering teams were working to reopen G216 while searching for survivors and missing people along the road and nearby river. Two helicopters have flown into the core area to deliver supplies and transport personnel and victims, while specialized drones are providing communications support. Basang Dondrub, a soldier from a unit of the Xizang Armed Police corps in Shigatse told China Daily that the force was continuing with road clearing and transportation work. "The machinery assisted in clearing roads and moving large rocks that couldn't be done manually. Meanwhile, personnel used shovels, pickaxes and their hands to dig and clear the ground and roads," he said. Meanwhile, the barrier lake that was formed above the Gyirong port has basically drained, the Ministry of Water Resources said on Sunday, citing drone footage and images captured in the morning. The ministry said an impact crater upstream of the barrier lake still warrants attention. Located about 5.6 km upstream at an altitude of around 3,700 meters, the crater is roughly 800 meters higher than the barrier lake. Authorities are using satellite remote sensing, radar, hydrological monitoring and video surveillance to monitor the lakes, river channels and surrounding slopes. Eighty-six specialists have been sent to identify possible secondary hazards. For evacuees, five temporary accommodation sites have been established, said Norbu Tsering, acting mayor of Shigatse. The city has mobilized 380 Party members and officials, township workers and medical staff members to provide round-the-clock assistance. Special arrangements have also been made for the elderly, children, pregnant women and infants, he said. Nyima Chozom, 28, from Kopa village in Salhe township, said she was cutting grass in a field on Wednesday when she saw debris rolling down the mountainside opposite her village. "It sounded deafening, almost like an earthquake," she said, adding that trees were swept away and objects outside her home shook violently. All eight members of her family were safely evacuated to a hotel. "We are safe now, and the conditions here are good," she said. She said most of her family's crops had already been harvested and she was reassured after learning that troops were helping villagers with farmwork. Wang Chao, deputy director of the disaster relief department of the Ministry of Emergency Management, said that more than 100,000 relief items had been allocated, enough to meet current rescue and resettlement needs. On Saturday, China Daily reporters arrived in Gyirong town, Xizang autonomous region, to report from the frontline of the debris-flow rescue operation. Multiple rescue teams are conducting searches in the hardest-hit areas, combing through mud and debris for those still unaccounted for. Search and rescue efforts are being carried out across land, water and air, with inflatable boats, ground teams and drones deployed for search, reconnaissance and the delivery of emergency supplies. Rescue operations continue as teams work to reach those in need in the affected areas. Nyima Chozom, a 28-year-old resident of Kopa village in Gyirong county, Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region, found safety and comfort at a relocation site after the mudslide. In an interview with China Daily, she recalled the terrifying moments when the disaster struck. As a mudslide struck Gyirong Port, border police officer Huang Peng remained at his post, guiding people to evacuate to safety. Since the catastrophic mudslide on Aug 26, veteran postman Basang Dundrub has been contributing to relief efforts at a temporary supply depot in Gyirong, Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region. Tasked with unloading rescue equipment and donated goods, Basang Dundrub helps ensure these essential supplies reach those in need. Having served China Post in Gyirong county for over a decade, Basang Dundrub volunteered for the relief mission immediately after the disaster struck. A parking lot has been transformed into a makeshift storage site, receiving firefighting and rescue equipment from Shigatse and donations from across the nation. Basang Dundrub and fellow volunteers begin work at 8 or 9 am, often continuing until the early hours of the next morning, leaving them with just a few hours of rest. "It's tiring, but when people are in difficulty, I should step forward and help," Basang Dundrub said. "As long as the relief work continues, I'll stay here." The massive mudslide, originating on the Nepalese side of the border, hit the Gyirong Port area on Aug 26. By 6 pm on Saturday, 16 people had been confirmed dead, and 546 remained missing, according to regional authorities. Drawing on previous emergency response experience, Basang Dundrub contacted his organization soon after the disaster and volunteered to help, knowing additional manpower would be needed. Ten postmen are currently involved in work in the disaster-hit area, including local employees and reinforcements from Shigatse, according to Basang Dundrub. The disaster also disrupted local postal services. Road restrictions halted deliveries for two days, resulting in a backlog of more than 1,300 pieces of mail and parcels, including university admission letters and other urgent deliveries. Postal workers coordinated with higher-level branches to resume services and clear the backlog. All the delayed items have since been delivered, Basang Dundrub said. For Basang Dundrub, ensuring important mail reaches people in remote communities has been part of the job for more than a decade. Basang Dundrub joined China Post in 2014, initially serving different townships before taking on delivery routes covering villages across Gyirong county. At one point, the routes covered 14 administrative villages in an area where mountainous terrain and unstable road conditions could turn routine deliveries into difficult journeys. Basang Dundrub recalled one occasion when difficult road conditions prevented the vehicle from reaching a remote village where a university admission letter needed to be delivered. Basang Dundrub continued part of the journey on foot. With limited mobile phone coverage and homes scattered across the area, Basang Dundrub sought help from local residents before eventually finding the student, Dorje Gyatso, and handing over the letter. "Dorje Gyatso's whole family was very happy," Basang Dundrub recalled. The family invited Basang Dundrub into their home and served butter tea and tsamba, a staple made from roasted barley flour. "Although the journey was difficult, seeing how happy they were when they received the letter made it worthwhile," Basang Dundrub said. Such challenges were common on the mountain routes. Basang Dundrub recalled another occasion when a vehicle broke down after dark, forcing Basang Dundrub to walk more than 10 kilometers before reaching a village and seeking help. Earlier this year, Basang Dundrub moved from frontline delivery into a role overseeing universal postal services at China Post's Gyirong county branch. Basang Dundrub was named a National Model Worker in 2025, an honor Basang Dundrub said represents greater responsibility. "The honor is not just a title. It represents people's trust in me," Basang Dundrub said. For now, that responsibility means remaining at the temporary supply depot, where trucks continue to arrive with equipment and donated goods. "I'll stay here until the disaster response is over," Basang Dundrub said. Communication signals have reached the core rescue area at Gyirong Port in Gyirong county, Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, after emergency base stations were set up to restore services disrupted by a deadly mudslide, local authorities said on Sunday. The first emergency base station near the border gate at Gyirong Port began operating at 1:30 pm on Sunday, Xinhua News Agency reported. Nyima Dorje, director of the Xizang Communications Administration, said a newly built base station at the forefront of road repair operations had successfully connected a call with rescuers at the port, marking the extension of communication coverage to the core rescue site. So far, telecommunications companies in Xizang have restored one damaged base station and built eight new ones. Two of the new stations were set up along the route from Gyirong county seat to Gyirong town, while six were built between Gyirong town and Gyirong Port. The restored communication network is expected to provide stronger support for rescue coordination and emergency operations in the disaster-hit area. The mudslide struck Gyirong Port on Wednesday morning after originating on the Nepalese side of the China-Nepal border, causing major casualties and leaving people missing. The disaster severely damaged infrastructure leading to the port, cutting off electricity and telecommunications services and complicating rescue operations. The Ministry of Natural Resources has fully launched risk and hazard investigations in the disaster-affected area in the Xizang autonomous region, identifying more than 60 potential geological hazard sites, eight of which have been classified as high risk, the ministry said on Sunday. The investigation follows a major debris flow triggered by an ice avalanche in Gyirong county on Aug 26. Since the disaster, the ministry has mobilized technical personnel from across the natural resources system, deploying four working groups equipped with drones, rangefinders and other survey instruments. The teams have focused on the ice avalanche source area, the barrier lake, debris flow channels and surrounding watersheds, conducting emergency surveying and mapping, as well as risk assessments, across the disaster-affected zone. The ministry has also intensified geological hazard patrols along emergency rescue routes, in nearby villages and at resettlement sites. It recommended combining drone aerial surveys with manual patrols to monitor risks during search and rescue operations. In addition, the ministry has organized more than 1,070 people, including technical professionals, grassroots officials and community-based monitoring volunteers, to expand investigations to more than 900 geological hazard sites across the broader area. On Sunday, the ministry convened a meeting to redeploy rescue and risk response efforts. The meeting heard opinions from academicians and experts and set out requirements for front-line risk management. It emphasized the importance of monitoring risks in the debris flow source area along the Cuojian River, a tributary where the ice collapse originated. It called for manual observation posts, integrated radar and video monitoring equipment, and microseismic sensors to be deployed on the opposite bank, working together to enable rapid early warning. Continuous risk assessment and monitoring were also required for potential collapses and landslides caused by channel scraping as the debris flow moved downstream. The meeting also recommended that the front-line command establish emergency shelters for rescue teams and designate emergency evacuation routes to ensure the safety of all personnel involved in rescue operations.

item.title: 7 minutes to disaster: glacier collapse triggers mudslide
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-31
7 minutes to disaster: glacier collapse triggers deadly mudslide Share - WeChat
From the catastrophic collapse of a glacier at 5,200 meters in Nepal to the debris flow crashing into the valley at Gyirong Port, roughly 1,800 meters above sea level, it took just seven minutes to cover 22 kilometers at an average speed of 50 meters per second. This mudslide was larger, faster, and more powerful, leaving downstream communities with an extremely narrow window to evacuate and causing even more devastating destruction and casualties.
